description: We are Team Krypthon, a multidisciplinary group of developers, engineers, and researchers passionate about building innovative, data-driven solutions for Earth observation. Led by a background in full-stack web engineering, cloud architecture, and AI, we are tackling "The Earth Information Jukebox" challenge. We are actively looking for passionate teammates with skills in Data Analysis, Python, and GIS / Earth Science to build an impactful prototype!
summary:
Echoes of Earth (The Earth Information Jukebox) is an interactive web experience that lets people see and hear twenty-three years (2003–2025) of Earth observations on a three-dimensional globe. We built it for NASA’s The Earth Information Jukebox challenge. Six planetary signals each have a distinct musical voice: Arctic and Antarctic sea ice, global surface temperature, atmospheric aerosols, vegetation greenness and precipitation. As the timeline advances, the data shapes pitch, harmony and tonal brightness, while NASA GIBS satellite imagery shows the same change on the planet.

The project answers the challenge by turning observational data into something people can experience as well as read. Arctic September sea ice shrinking by 42% between 2003 and 2012 becomes a sound that audibly thins, and warming that reaches a record +1.29 °C in 2024 becomes rising musical tension. This matters because climate data is vast and hard to read, and sound helps slow, large-scale change register with students, educators and the public, including audiences who struggle with charts.
details:
1. What it does and how it works

Echoes of Earth (The Earth Information Jukebox) is a browser application that visualizes and sonifies Earth observation data across six domains. A custom-shaded WebGL globe, built with Three.js, displays each domain. A Tone.js audio engine converts each year’s value into music, using a scale chosen for each signal (for example, Dorian harmonies for aerosols and Lydian for vegetation and rainfall). The data drives pitch, filter brightness, reverberation and stereo placement.

Users can explore in several ways:

  • Timeline: play or scrub through 2003–2025, with highlighted moments such as the 2012 Arctic record low, the 2007 steepest drop and the 2013 rebound.
  • 3D Split Curtain: drag a live divider across the globe to compare 2003 with any later year.
  • Acoustic buoys: click the globe to deploy a buoy that sounds the local value. Buoys are saved per session, and each location is reverse-geocoded to a place name.
  • Snapshots: save a view as a shareable link.
  • Upload CSV: overlay a year, value dataset next to the NASA series.
  • Export: WebM video with audio, and standard MIDI files.

2. Data, methods and provenance

Arctic and Antarctic sea ice

  • Source: NSIDC Sea Ice Index v4
  • Measure: September extent (million km²)

Temperature

  • Source: NASA GISS GISTEMP v4
  • Measure: annual anomaly vs 1951–1980 (°C)

Air

  • Source: NASA MODIS Terra C6.1 (MOD08_M3)
  • Measure: annual mean aerosol optical depth, 550 nm

Greenness

  • Source: NASA MODIS Terra C6.1 (MOD13C2)
  • Measure: annual mean NDVI over vegetated land

Rainfall

  • Source: NOAA/NASA GPCP v2.3
  • Measure: annual mean precipitation (mm/day)

The aerosol, greenness and rainfall series are 12-month, cosine-latitude area-weighted means, computed from 552 MODIS files and 276 rainfall grids.

  • data/PROVENANCE.md lists every satellite file used, and the README documents each method.
  • Overlays come from NASA GIBS.

3. Benefits

  • Perception: slow trends become audible patterns that complement charts.
  • Accessibility: spoken captions, a simplified interface and screen-reader labels.
  • Education: Classroom mode with teacher notes, plus CSV upload so students can compare their own data with NASA’s.
  • Creative reuse: MIDI and video export for musicians, artists and advocates.
  • Resilience: it is installable and works offline after the first visit.

4. Intended impact

To make Earth observations something people feel as well as read, and so deepen public and student engagement with climate change and planetary health.

5. Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: JavaScript (ES6 modules, no bundler), Three.js with custom GLSL shaders, Tone.js, GSAP, lil-gui, HTML and CSS, and a service-worker PWA.
  • Backend: Node.js 22.5+ with the built-in node:sqlite (WAL mode) and zero npm dependencies. REST endpoints serve metrics, regions, buoys, snapshots, geocoding and a disk-caching proxy for NASA GIBS imagery.
  • Data processing: Python with earthaccess, pyhdf and numpy, working on HDF4 and NetCDF files.
  • Quality: an automated test suite (8 API tests) and a parity script that checks every dataset copy.

6. Creativity

The Earth becomes an instrument. The data is the score, the globe is the stage, and users reach into it with buoys and the split curtain. Each domain has its own musical character, so the result is composition rather than generic data beeps.

7. Factors considered

  • Data integrity: every series carries its true source and method, with a file-level provenance record.
  • Accessibility and cognitive load: spoken captions, a Simple UI layout and Classroom mode.
  • Reliability: ventured libraries and textures, a service-worker cache, a procedural texture fallback, and a disk cache for imagery.
  • Simplicity: a dependency-free backend. Run it with npm start and open http://localhost:3000.

8. Limitations and future work

  • The series are global means, so regional detail comes from the imagery layers rather than the numbers.
  • MODIS Terra has known late-mission calibration drift, which the 2025 aerosol value may reflect.
  • Place names for buoys need an internet connection.
  • Next steps: add more NASA datasets such as sea level and atmospheric CO₂, add regional averages, and run listening tests with visually impaired users.

9. Team, links and license
